name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,466

clue.text: A once perhaps outgoing girl snorting Charlie

definitions.note: an example of the answer: A was a grade in the old ABC1 classification

indicators.note: whoever snorts something takes it in, so one piece is drawn inside the other phrase

blocks.note: an outgoing person is sociable, social
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet, and slang for cocaine
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A party girl who once took cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: The outgoing girl is SOCIAL LASS, and she takes in C to make SOCIAL CLASS. Britain's old ABC1 market research scheme put people into classes A, B, C1 and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: Grade A was the top band of the old British demographic grading scheme, an example of such a group.

clue.text: S&M article, one that'll knock you out!

blocks.note: read out as S and M
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An item of bondage gear that packs a punch.
explanation.walkthrough: S&M is read in full as S AND M, then the article AN follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sandman of folklore sprinkles sand to send children to sleep, so he puts you out cold.

clue.text: One holding a slug caught by game bird without crest

indicators.note: a crest is the top of something, so the bird loses its first letter

blocks.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a partridge is a game bird

explanation.surface: Something holding a slug is caught by a pheasant-like bird with no crest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slug' suggests a garden pest, but it is a bullet, and a cartridge holds one.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartridge is the casing that contains a bullet, and slug is slang for a bullet or shotgun projectile.

clue.text: A cottage for George Michael and those who might sell it?

blocks.note: taken as written
a cottage is British slang for a public lavatory used for gay encounters; the singer George Michael was arrested in one in 1998

explanation.surface: A country cottage, and the people who might sell it for a pop star.
explanation.walkthrough: The gents is a men's public toilet. The 'it' is the cottage, sold by estate agents.
explanation.definitionFit: Estate agents are the people who sell property such as a cottage on an owner's behalf.

clue.text: A cool chest to be redesigned in brown colours

indicators.note: something redesigned is rebuilt to a new plan, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A cool box being restyled in shades of brown.
explanation.definitionFit: Chocolate is a dark brown shade, so chocolates are a range of those deep brown tones.

clue.text: A red pine

blocks.note: taken as written
Che Guevara, the revolutionary, is a famous red

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a coloured tree; 'pine' is the verb meaning to long for.
explanation.definitionFit: To pine for something is to yearn for it, and to ache for it has the same meaning of longing.

clue.text: Small cape, jumper and golf tops in extra small? They're tight!

indicators.note: the tops of words are their opening letters, so only the heads of the next two words count

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
C is the map abbreviation for cape
a roo, or kangaroo, is a jumper
golf is G in the NATO alphabet
the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A list of clothes in size extra small, which are naturally tight.
explanation.walkthrough: Cape, jumper and tops all look like clothing; a jumper is a sweater in Britain, but here it is a kangaroo. 'Tight' means stingy.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrooge is a miser, named after Dickens's character, and tight is slang for mean with money.

clue.text: Hoskins is one to get half-cut with plonk

indicators.note: cutting something in half leaves only one half, so the back half of the word goes

blocks.note: Hoskins is the compiler of this puzzle

explanation.surface: The setter admits he gets tipsy on cheap wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' (drunk) and 'plonk' (cheap wine) paint a boozy picture; plonk is the verb meaning to put down.
explanation.definitionFit: To plonk something is to put it down heavily, and to set it down means placing it.

clue.text: Fire encircling north Sandwich?

indicators.note: something encircling goes all the way round, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: to fire someone is to sack them
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Flames around north Sandwich, the Kentish town.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandwich is a town in Kent, which makes 'north' look like a direction; the question mark marks a sandwich as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandwich is a typical light meal eaten between main meals, an example of this.

clue.text: Aristocrats bearing drugs? They're sweeties!

indicators.note: to bear something is to carry it, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: toffs are posh people
E is ecstasy, twice for the plural

explanation.surface: Posh people carrying drugs turn out to be lovely people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweeties' reads as darlings, but here it is the British word for sweets, candy.
explanation.definitionFit: Toffees are chewy candies made from boiled sugar and butter, which British children call sweeties.

clue.text: Tend to swear if leader turns nationalist

indicators.note: the leader is the first letter, and turning it means it becomes a different letter

blocks.note: to curse is to swear
N is the abbreviation for nationalist

explanation.surface: Someone tends to swear whenever their leader becomes a nationalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tend to' looks like a phrase meaning 'be inclined to'; the definition is 'Tend' alone, as in tending the sick.
explanation.definitionFit: To nurse someone is to care for them, and to tend a patient means looking after them.

clue.text: Short rest then 45 mins of footie, mate?

indicators.note: something short is cut down, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: the rest are the others
a football match has two halves of 45 minutes

explanation.surface: A quick break, then one half of a football match, pal?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mate' sounds like a footballing pal, but it means a partner or spouse; footie is British slang for football.
explanation.definitionFit: Your other half is an informal idiom for a spouse or partner, and mate means a life partner too.

clue.text: Hit back at husband performing arduous task

indicators.note: going back means reading the word from end to start

blocks.note: to ram is to hit
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for husband
an actor performing is on

explanation.surface: Hitting back at a husband who is struggling with a hard job.
explanation.definitionFit: A marathon is figuratively any long, exhausting undertaking, after the 26-mile race.

clue.text: You're not posh around Kelvin and I, dog

indicators.note: a word placed around others surrounds them

blocks.note: an informal, non-U spelling of you're
K is the symbol for kelvin
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tells a snob called Kelvin they are no better than a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posh' and 'not posh' echo the old U and non-U split of British speech; YORE stands for a common way of writing you're.
explanation.definitionFit: A Yorkie is the familiar name for a Yorkshire terrier, a small breed of dog.

clue.text: Measure up Spurs teams for a complete makeover

indicators.note: a complete makeover changes everything about how something is arranged, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange; Spurs is Tottenham Hotspur football club

explanation.surface: Tottenham's sides need a total overhaul to come up to standard.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass muster is an idiom for being good enough, reaching the standard required on inspection.

clue.text: Ecstasy and horse knocked back out of habit?

indicators.note: knocked back means sent backwards, so the letters are read from the end

blocks.note: E is the drug ecstasy
a dun is a greyish-brown horse

explanation.surface: Taking drugs and downing horse, heroin, purely out of habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of habit' reads as 'by routine', but a habit is a nun's robe, and a nun out of it is undressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone stripped of their habit, the religious garment, is left without clothes, the idea of being naked.

clue.text: Chap greases up for woman who's the boss

indicators.note: things that are up are disturbed and in disorder, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: a chap is a man
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A man sucks up to his female boss.
explanation.walkthrough: To grease up to someone sounds like flattery; 'up' is the signal to jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Manageress is the older female form of manager, someone in charge of a shop or business.

clue.text: Weed out of car and I teed head of AA off

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter
something gone off has spoiled, so the letters are put out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
the first letter of the motoring organisation

explanation.surface: Someone leaves their car and tees off from a golf course with the AA's patrolman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weed out of' looks like the definition; 'of' only links. The AA is Britain's Automobile Association, the breakdown service.
explanation.definitionFit: To weed something out is to remove it completely, and to eradicate means wiping it out entirely.

clue.text: Fixed up couple with grass for an overcoat

indicators.note: an overcoat is worn outside, so one piece covers the other

blocks.note: a reed is a tall grass
a couple is a pair

explanation.surface: A couple patched up with straw as a coat.
explanation.definitionFit: Something repaired has been mended, and to fix up a broken item means restoring it.

clue.text: Go before red escapee goes to pieces

indicators.note: going to pieces means falling apart, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A communist escapee panics and leaves first.
explanation.definitionFit: To predecease someone is to die earlier than them; to go before is a euphemism for dying first.

clue.text: Writer with spirit taking on university publisher

indicators.note: taking something on means admitting it, so the letter is drawn inside

blocks.note: a pen is a writing tool
gin is a spirit
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: An author with plenty of spirit getting work from a university publisher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' reads as an author, but it is the writing tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Penguin Books is a well-known British paperback publishing house, famous for its orange covers.

clue.text: God may absolve really stupid leaders

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their opening letters

blocks.note: the opening letters of these four words

explanation.surface: God may forgive even the most foolish rulers.
explanation.definitionFit: Mars was the Roman deity of war, so he is one of the classical gods.

clue.text: Teachers screening Aliens upset relatives

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the word reads from the bottom
to screen something is to hide it behind or within, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: pupils call male teachers sir
ETs are extra-terrestrials

explanation.surface: Teachers showing alien films upset the family.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools pupils address a male teacher as sir.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisters are female siblings, members of the same family and so close relatives.

clue.text: Necks special caffeine drinks, being energy-sapped

indicators.note: sapped of energy means losing every E, the symbol for energy

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for special
coffees are drinks containing caffeine

explanation.surface: Someone gulps down special energy drinks and still feels drained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Necks' looks like a noun but is British slang for drinking quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: To neck food or drink is to gulp it down greedily, as to scoff means eating fast.

clue.text: Approach grasping old fellow? Definitely not!

indicators.note: something grasping holds on tight, so one piece takes in the others

blocks.note: to approach is to near
O is the abbreviation for old
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: Someone is asked whether they will approach a dodgy old man, and refuses.
explanation.walkthrough: No fear is a British exclamation of flat refusal.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom expresses emphatic refusal, the colloquial equivalent of saying there is no chance.

clue.text: Damn fine magistrate that's released Juliet

indicators.note: releasing something lets it go, so that letter leaves the word

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
a magistrate is a judge
Juliet is J in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A damned fine magistrate who freed Juliet from custody.
explanation.definitionFit: Fudge is a mild exclamation of annoyance, a polite substitute for a curse word.

clue.text: Hen parties with music and light bites

indicators.note: to party is to live it up wildly, so these letters go into disorder

blocks.note: the first letters to rearrange
the rest of the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Hen nights with music and nibbles.
explanation.walkthrough: A hen party is a British bachelorette party, but 'parties' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: Munchies is an informal word for snacks, small things to nibble between meals.

clue.text: Save the foremost of Serengeti watering-holes

indicators.note: the foremost letter of a word is its first one

blocks.note: save and bar both mean except
its opening letter

explanation.surface: Conserving the main water sources of the African plain.
explanation.walkthrough: The Serengeti sets up a picture of animals at waterholes; a watering-hole is also slang for a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Watering-hole is jocular slang for a pub where people drink, and bars serve drinks.

clue.text: A French character squeezing flipping red cow's udder?

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the word is read backwards
squeezing means holding tight in between, so one piece sits inside the others

blocks.note: the French masculine word for a
an actor's character is a part
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Frenchman milking a cow with irritable language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' could be a mild oath before 'red cow'; it is the turnaround signal. The question mark shows the udder is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: An udder hangs from the belly of a cow, so it is an example of an animal's lower body part.

clue.text: Perhaps Trump and his kind of news baffles Liberal

indicators.note: a baffle is a screen that blocks, so one piece shuts the other inside

blocks.note: Donald Trump popularised the phrase fake news
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: Trump and his brand of news confuse the liberals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baffles' looks like confuses, but it means encloses.
explanation.definitionFit: A flake is slang for an unreliable or eccentric person, and the setter offers Trump as one example.

clue.text: Born Miss, but getting the chop finally

indicators.note: chopping at the final position means the last letter is cut off

blocks.note: to miss something is to need it

explanation.surface: A woman born a Miss, until she was dumped at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Born Miss' suggests a maiden name, the very use of the answer, but 'Miss' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Née, from French, means born and introduces a married woman's maiden surname.

clue.text: We're suspicious of cleaners seen around one half of street

definitions.note: a clause standing for the plural noun: those who say this

indicators.note: seen around something means wrapped about it, so one piece encloses the others
taking only half of a word drops the remainder

blocks.note: dusters are cleaning cloths
I is the Roman numeral one
the word to be halved

explanation.surface: Residents are wary of cleaners lurking around their street.
explanation.definitionFit: Distrusters are people who doubt others, so as a group they would describe themselves as wary.
